name: Codon Usage Calculator
seoDesc: Codon usage is how often each of the 61 sense codons appears in a coding sequence. Free codon usage calculator: enter your values and get complete codons, gc
summary:
Codon usage is how often each of the 61 sense codons appears in a coding sequence. It returns complete codons, gc at the third position, stop codons, different codons used and rare codons, and the panel shows all of them at once.

Because several codons stand for the same amino acid, the pattern shows which synonyms a gene prefers — the first thing to check before expressing a gene in E. coli, yeast or CHO cells, where rare codons stall the ribosome. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Codon Usage
sections.html:
RSCU = observed count of a codon ÷ (count of its amino acid ÷ number of its synonyms). GC3 = codons ending in G or C ÷ complete codons × 100

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
RSCUrelative synonymous codon usage; 1.0 = no preference—
GC3GC content at the third codon position%
CDScoding sequence, in frame from the start codon—

sections.title: How do I use the Codon Usage?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
RSCU > 1.5Strongly preferredthe codon is used far more than chance in this gene
RSCU 0.8 – 1.5Neutralno meaningful preference
RSCU < 0.5Avoideda candidate rare codon if the host also dislikes it
GC3 > 70%GC-rich coding sequencecommon in Streptomyces, Mycobacterium, some plants

  • RSCU normalises for family size: serine has six codons, methionine and tryptophan have one, so raw counts cannot be compared without it.

  • The rare-codon count only looks at families that appear at least five times. In a short sequence most amino acids occur once, so every codon is trivially 100% of its family and a plain 10% cut-off would report nothing.

  • Codon usage is species-specific. A codon that is common in humans can be rare in E. coli, which is why a human cDNA often expresses poorly in bacteria.

  • Rare codons do not always slow translation — clusters of them, especially at the 5′ end, are the ones that matter.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Analysing the sequence in the wrong frame, which turns every codon into noise.
  • Including the stop codon in the GC3 figure while excluding it from the codon table.
  • Comparing a gene's usage with a host table built from highly expressed genes rather than from the whole genome.

faq.q: What is a good GC3 value?
faq.a: There is no good or bad value — it is a fingerprint of the organism. E. coli sits near 55%, human genes near 60%, and Plasmodium near 25%.

faq.q: Why does codon usage matter for expression?
faq.a: Rare codons can exhaust the matching tRNA, cause ribosome stalling and lower yield. Codon optimisation replaces them with common synonyms without changing the protein.

faq.q: Should I include the stop codon?
faq.a: Analyse it separately. Stops carry no amino acid, so they have no RSCU within a family.

faq.q: What does the Codon Usage actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns complete codons, gc at the third position, stop codons, different codons used and rare codons. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
